newsitem.title: RWANDA: Multinational reconnaissance team to enter Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Multinational reconnaissance team to enter Zaire.

text.p: A multinational operation to help hundreds of thousands of Rwandan refugees adrift in east Zaire makes one step forward this weekend when a small military team goes in on reconnaissance, a Canadian spokesman said on Friday.
In Ottawa on Thursday, Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said that ambassadors from over 20 countries would meet on Friday to give the multinational operation final approval.

"We have now achieved an agreement," he said in a statement. The agreement is to set up a multinational headquarters in Uganda, pursue further reconnaissance and put in place a capability to airdrop food in eastern Zaire if needed.

The Canadian spokesman in central Africa, Major Paul Dangerfield, said on Friday that the reconnaissance team would include two or three officers going into eastern Zaire with the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR to find out where the refugees are.
"They will be unarmed and out of uniform and we expect them to go in on Saturday or Sunday," he told reporters in the Rwandan capital Kigali.
Different agencies and governments have given widely varying accounts of the number and location of the refugees, in some cases for partisan reasons.

The Rwandan government and the Zairean rebels who now control large parts of eastern Zaire oppose the deployment of an international force, which might indirectly strengthen the position of ailing Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko.

They also argue that since fighting broke out in eastern Zaire in October most of the Rwandan refugees have either returned home or are trying to do so, making the multinational operation largely redundant.
In an interview to be published on Monday in the Paris-based weekly Nouvel Afrique Asie, rebel leader Laurent Kabila said his men would resist any French presence in a military force.
"Let no one believe any longer that we'll keep our arms folded when we see the first French soldier or paratrooper in this region," he said.
France said on Thursday the number of refugees still made a multinational ground force necessary but it was also prepared to join a proposed airdrop of food into eastern Zaire.
The airdrop proposal was designed to circumvent objections to a ground force but the government of Zaire added to the controversy on Thursday by rejecting this alternative.
Zairean government spokesman Boguo Makeli said Zaire was worried the airdrops would not be safe and would be staged from neighbouring countries it accuses of aggression.
"Zaire will not authorise overflights of its territory by any aircraft, whichever force it belongs to, for an operation so dangerous for the people concerned," he told Reuters.
On the ground in eastern Zaire, a column of refugees continued to reach the town of Sake on their way to the Rwandan border, 30 km (20 miles) to the east.
UNHCR will bring 700 of them from Sake to the border town of Goma in a convoy of trucks on Friday, UNHCR officials said.

The Canadian commander of the proposed multinational force, Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril, told UNHCR in Goma on Thursday he estimated there were between 100,000 and 150,000 Rwandan refugees in a single concentration around the village of Numbi, 40 km (25 miles) southwest of Goma.
Numbi is inaccessible because the road is blocked by vehicles and is reported to be mined.
Estimates of the total number of refugees have varied from about 200,000 to more than 600,000.
